Charismatic Renewal
kar-iz-MAT-ik rih-NOO-uhl
noun (modern movement)
From Greek charisma, a gift of grace (plural charismata), the term Paul uses for the Spirit's gifts (1 Cor 12); renewal from Latin renovare, to make new again.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Charismatic Renewal is the mid-twentieth-century movement that carried Pentecostal practice — tongues, prophecy, healing — out of the Pentecostal denominations and into mainline Protestant and Roman Catholic churches, beginning in the 1960s. From it later grew the New Apostolic Reformation, the International House of Prayer (IHOP), and the ministries gathered around Bethel Church, with their claim to restored offices of apostle and prophet and their continuous "words from the Lord." This dictionary acknowledges that many caught up in the Renewal sought a deeper devotion than the dead formalism around them, and that desire is not to be despised. Yet the movement's defining claim — that modern apostles and prophets speak fresh revelation today — strikes at the closed canon. The apostles were eyewitnesses of the risen Christ, appointed to lay the foundation once (Eph 2:20; Acts 1:21-22); their office cannot be reconstituted. To "prophesy" alongside Scripture is to add to the Word that God has finished, against the warning "Add thou not unto his words" (Prov 30:6). This dictionary confesses cessationism: God's public revelation is complete in the sixty-six books, and no man may claim apostolic authority or fresh prophetic oracles in this age.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A movement from the 1960s carrying Pentecostal practice into mainline and Roman Catholic churches, later producing the New Apostolic Reformation, IHOP, and Bethel. Its claim of modern apostles and prophets corrupts the closed canon.

CHARISMATIC RENEWAL, noun. A twentieth-century movement importing tongues, prophecy, and healing into established Protestant and Roman communions.

Its later forms claim to restore the offices of apostle and prophet.

"Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar" (Prov 30:6).

The apostolic office was founded on eyewitness of the risen Christ and cannot be repeated.

Where new oracles are claimed, the sufficiency of the closed canon is denied.

📖 Key Scripture

Eph 2:20 — "And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;"

Prov 30:6 — "Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar."

Acts 1:22 — "Beginning from the baptism of John, unto that same day that he was taken up from us, must one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection."

Heb 1:1 — "God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets,"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Renewal and its New Apostolic offshoots claim living apostles and prophets bearing fresh revelation, adding to the finished Word and denying the closed canon.

expand to see more

The gravest error is the claim to a restored apostolate. An apostle, in the New Testament sense, was an eyewitness of the resurrection commissioned directly by Christ to lay the church's foundation (Acts 1:21-22; Eph 2:20). That foundation is laid once. When modern movements ordain "apostles" and receive ongoing "prophetic words," they treat the canon as still open and the Scriptures as a beginning rather than a completed deposit. The warning stands: "Add thou not unto his words" (Prov 30:6).

The Renewal's spread into Roman Catholicism compounded the confusion, for it grafted experiential gifts onto a system that already denies sola fide and exalts a treasury of merit. The later excesses — IHOP's ceaseless "prophetic" output, Bethel's signs-and-wonders culture, the New Apostolic Reformation's governmental apostles — are sober concerns, not mere differences of style. This dictionary honors the longing for the living God that drew many in, while confessing that He is found not in fresh oracles but in His finished Word, "in these last days spoken unto us by his Son" (Heb 1:2).

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name comes from charismata, Paul's word for the Spirit's gifts, which the movement claims to recover in full apostolic measure.

expand to see more

Greek charisma, a grace-gift; plural charismata in 1 Cor 12.

Renewal signals a claimed revival of those gifts in the wider church.

The movement reads 1 Corinthians 12-14 as binding on every age alike.

Cessationists read the same chapters as describing the apostolic foundation now laid.

Where apostles and prophets are claimed anew, the closed canon is at stake.

Usage

"The Charismatic Renewal swept into mainline parishes that had grown cold and formal."

"Critics of the Charismatic Renewal point first to its claim of living apostles."

"The New Apostolic Reformation is the most far-reaching offshoot of the Charismatic Renewal."
